name: Venera 6
payload: Flight bus and atmospheric probe (1,130 kg; probe 405 kg)
significance: Venera 6 reached Venus a day after its twin Venera 5, so the two probes could check each other's readings. Its probe descended for 51 minutes on 17 May 1969 and was lost at the same pressure as Venera 5, 27 atmospheres, but at a lower altitude, a hint that it had come down over high ground. Published by Soviet scientists in March 1970, the two missions sharpened Venera 4's findings: an atmosphere about 97% carbon dioxide, under 2% nitrogen and almost no oxygen, with a surface far hotter and more crushing than anywhere on Earth.
statusNote: Launched 1969-01-10 05:51:52 UT on a Molniya-M from Tyuratam (Siddiqi). Mid-course correction on 1969-03-16. The probe separated 25,000 km from Venus and entered the atmosphere at 06:05 UT on 1969-05-17 at 11.17 km/s; 51 min of descent data until contact was lost at 27 atm, at 5 S, 23 E. TRAJECTORY (calculated, drawn dashed): no measured trajectory for this spacecraft is publicly archived (JPL Horizons has no ephemeris for it), so the path is a two-body transfer orbit calculated between Earth at the published launch time and Venus at the published arrival time. For modern direct flights checked against Horizons, arcs calculated this way fall within about 0.002 AU (300,000 km) of the real trajectory, but this one can't be checked against data, so it's drawn dashed.
